claim: Israel was imposed on the land by outside powers, and the Jews took the land by force in 1948.

heard.who: Rashid Khalidi, historian, in a 2024 interview
heard.quote: pushing through the partition resolution, which is the birth certificate of the state of Israel, the 1947 General Assembly resolution, partitioning Palestine

answer: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937; Arab leaders rejected it, and the Zionist Congress rejected its borders but allowed talks. On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13. The Jewish state would have had about 56 percent of the land (UNSCOP's version put the whole Negev semi-desert in it), when Jews were about a third of the people and held about 6 percent by Mandate-government ownership figures; Imseis counts Arabs as owning 48 percent. The Jewish Agency accepted; Palestinian Arab leaders rejected the plan. Fighting began at once. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and Arab armies entered on 15 May. By 1949 Israel held about 78 percent of the former mandate.

could_not_verify: The text of the Peel report itself: the Avalon page did not load. Peel is cited only through reference works and a UN secretariat paper.
The peace offer in Israel's declaration of independence: Avalon's text has it, but I found no second readable page, so I left it out of the facts.

Fact on the Arab League cable (15 May 1948): worded as what the cable says, with the cable itself as the record. I looked for a reliable reader of it (Imseis, the Israel Law Review report, Britannica, Shlaim's chapter, the US State Department's milestone page, FRUS 1948 vol. V d281) and found none that reports its content in a readable form; the US telegram (FRUS d281) summarises it but is a government source. A person should read a monograph on the 1948 war (Morris, 1948; Rogan and Shlaim, The War for Palestine) on what the cable said, and the Security Council record of 20 and 26 May 1948.

Transjordan's dissent (Abdullah's understanding with the Jewish Agency): still rests on Shlaim and Karsh, who are the two sides of the dispute. Britannica's Abdullah and Jordan pages did not load. A person should read Rogan and Shlaim, The War for Palestine, and Morris, 1948.
Population at end of 1946 (record fact): the record is UNSCOP's report and Imseis cites it in a footnote; I found no second reliable reader.

Land ownership (record fact): the record is the Mandate government's Village Statistics of 1945, read in Sami Hadawi's 1970 reprint (PLO Research Center), because I found no readable copy of the original; Imseis is the only reliable reader. Hadawi's own table puts Arab ownership at 48.5 percent but public land at about 40 percent, which does not match Imseis's 'the remainder'; the table is garbled in the text I could read. A person should read the Survey of Palestine vol. I and the Ad Hoc Committee's sub-committee 2 report (A/AC.14/32, appendix VI) and settle the public-land share.

How much of the Jewish state was the Negev: no scholarly or UN source I could read gives a percentage. UNSCOP's report puts the whole Beersheba sub-district in the Jewish state and calls it semidesert and nearly half of Palestine, but the resolution's final boundaries differ in detail. The 'about 60 percent' figure is advocacy and stays in contested. A person should measure the Resolution 181 maps.
The 70 percent state-land figure (Jewish Virtual Library) refers only to land in what became Israel; I found no reliable source for it and it stays in contested.

Claims that Jewish forces took territory beyond the plan before 15 May appear on a UN Division for Palestinian Rights page, which counts as advocacy; I found no independent readable source and omitted it.
Khalidi's book is not cited (no authorised readable copy); his 2024 interview is used.
Dissent among Arab states beyond Transjordan (for example Egypt's and Syria's reluctance): I did not find a readable source.
Relabelled as 'other' (no named author or institution): History Skills, Explaining History, OnWar, Fanack, War History Online.

Facts that do not meet the gate's source rule: the Arab League cable (the record, no reliable reader), Transjordan (two scholars on opposite sides), the 1946 population (the record plus one reader), the 1945 land ownership (the record plus one reader).

FINAL REVIEW (2026-11-20): reader gaps under the record rule. Fact 11 (Arab League cable): record read and quoted correctly, but no reliable reader (the two others are 'other' sites; the record is cited twice). Fact 14 (land): record read only in Hadawi's PLO Research Center reprint; one reader (Imseis). Hadawi's table (garbled in the text I could read) puts Arab ownership at 48.50 percent and public land at 40.16 percent, so Imseis's 'the remainder being publicly owned' does not match it and was taken out of the fact. Fact 15 (1946 population): record read; one reader (Imseis). Fact 16 (Mandate Article 6): the Fordham page is another copy of the text, not a reader; only UNSCOP quotes it. Facts 2-5 lean on a Lumen Learning course page (anonymous textbook text) as a reader. A person should find a scholarly reader for each of facts 11, 14, 15, or accept them as record-only.
not_claimed: This card does not claim the UN vote made the 1948 war or the later displacement of Palestinians right, wrong or inevitable.
It does not claim the vote was free of great-power pressure or that Palestinian Arabs were consulted in the way they wanted.
It does not claim Jewish forces took only land the plan gave them; Israel ended up with more.
It does not say who fired first in the civil war that followed the vote.

answer_claims.says: The idea of splitting Palestine came first from a British commission in 1937; Arab leaders rejected it, and the Zionist Congress rejected its borders but allowed talks.
On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended a Jewish state and an Arab state, by 33 votes to 13.

The Jewish state would have had about 56 percent of the land (UNSCOP's version put the whole Negev semi-desert in it), when Jews were about a third of the people and held about 6 percent by Mandate-government ownership figures; Imseis counts Arabs as owning 48 percent.
The Jewish Agency accepted; Palestinian Arab leaders rejected the plan.
Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and Arab armies entered on 15 May.
By 1949 Israel held about 78 percent of the former mandate.

skeptic.notes: Final review after the record rule. Read the records: Resolution 181 (Avalon), the Assembly's 29 Nov 1947 vote record ('adopted by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions'; Saudi Arabia's 'does not consider itself bound' and its 'pressure ... by some of the big powers' remark are there), UNSCOP's report (1,203,000 / 608,000 / 35,000 / 1,846,000, 'settled', Muslim share 75 to 60 percent; Beersheba sub-district; 'increased almost entirely' natural), the Arab League cable (S/745), Hadawi's reprint of the Village Statistics, and the Mandate. Record flags: facts 2, 3, 15, 16 are worded as what the record says and the flag is honest. Fact 11 is worded as what the cable says (flag honest) but has NO reader; fact 14 and fact 15 have one reader each (Imseis), so they do not meet the record rule in substance; the gate fails them too. Fixed by me: (must-fix, done) fact 13 said the Jewish state 'would have included the whole Negev desert'; that is UNSCOP's proposal, and the Assembly's boundary text for the Arab state runs through part of the Beersheba sub-district, so it is now worded as UNSCOP's report; the answer follows. (must-fix, done) fact 14 repeated Imseis's 'remainder publicly owned', which Hadawi's table contradicts (public land 40.16 percent, Arab 48.50 percent); removed from the fact and the answer.
